title: Sain ajan nopeasti
subtitle: The big picture behind palvelua and ajan

blocks.text: Sain ajan nopeasti has sat in your dialogues since Lesson 8, right alongside sain hyvää palvelua from Lesson 1. Ajan and palvelua are doing the exact same grammatical job — both are objects — but they end differently. This lesson finally explains why, and it's one of the most useful patterns in the whole language.

blocks.title: Complete vs. in-progress, baked into grammar
blocks.text: Finnish grammar makes a distinction English doesn't mark at all: was the object fully, definitely obtained/affected, or only partially/some of it/ongoing? Ajan (an appointment, Lesson 8) is one whole thing you definitely got. Palvelua (Lesson 1) is more like an uncountable quality you received some of. The ending tells you which, instantly.
Piece 1 — Partitive object: partial, ongoing, or uncountable

blocks.content: The {partitive|grammar|case name|some of/partial} object marks something uncountable, indefinite in amount, or an action still in progress. Sain hyvää {palvelua|grammar|partitive object|service} — 'I got good service' — palvelu is mass-noun-like here, not one countable thing you fully consumed.

items.en: I was waiting for the car (ongoing, not yet resolved).

blocks.text: Piece 2 — Accusative object: one whole, complete thing

blocks.content: The {accusative|grammar|case name|total/complete} object marks a single, definite, fully-affected thing — usually ending in -n for singular nouns, the same shape as the genitive you learned in Lesson 12. Sain {ajan|grammar|accusative, total object|an appointment} nopeasti — one specific appointment, fully obtained, done.

items.en: I changed the part (the whole part, completely).

blocks.text: Piece 3 — Three triggers that force the partitive

blocks.title: You've already met all three triggers
blocks.text: You now have every piece needed to predict which case an object takes. Three things always force partitive, no exceptions: negation (Lesson 3 — ei ilmennyt {ongelmia|grammar|partitive, forced by negation|problems}), a number of 2 or more (Lesson 19 — kolme {kertaa|grammar|partitive, forced by number|times}), and an incomplete/uncountable object like today's palvelua. Anywhere none of those three apply, and the object is one whole, specific thing, reach for the accusative -n instead.

lines.speaker: A
lines.en: Did you get an appointment quickly?

lines.speaker: B
lines.fi: Kyllä, ja sain myös hyvää palvelua.
lines.en: Yes, and I also got good service.

lines.speaker: B
lines.fi: Kyllä, korjasivat vian, eikä ongelmia ilmennyt sen jälkeen.
lines.en: Yes, they fixed the fault, and no problems appeared after that.

blocks.title: Paul Noble Rule
blocks.text: One question decides the ending: is the object whole, specific, and fully affected? If yes — accusative -n. If it's negated, plural-counted, or vague/uncountable — partitive. Run every object you meet from now on through that single question, and the case almost always follows.

blocks.content: Ajan: A-jan (short, the 'j' is a 'y' sound). Palvelua: PAL-ve-lu-a (four syllables, the final -a is light). Osan vs osaa: O-san (crisp final n, accusative) vs O-saa (held final vowel, partitive) — that length difference is the whole signal.

rows.en: marks a whole, complete, specific object
marks partial, ongoing, uncountable, negated, or counted (2+) objects
